items.title: NBA investigation ends with LA Clippers sent 25 seasons back in time
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
The NBA’s nearly year-long investigation into the Los Angeles Clippers has ended with one of the harshest punishments in league history, sending the franchise back to territory last seen during Minnesota’s Joe Smith salary-cap scandal 25 seasons ago.

The League has concluded that the Clippers violated salary-cap circumvention rules by facilitating endorsement deals for Kawhi Leonard with Aspiration, Boingo Wireless, Daktronics and Lockton Insurance, as first reported by ESPN’s Shams Charania.

The investigation began after reporting by Torre, and the process was conducted by Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz.

The sanctions immediately reshape the Clippers’ already-long-gone future:

  • The Clippers have been fined $30 million, the largest team fine in NBA history.
  • Los Angeles is losing its first-round picks in 2029, 2030, 2031, 2032 and 2033.
  • The Clippers have been placed under a five-year compliance and monitoring program.
  • Owner Steve Ballmer has been suspended from all league and team activities for one year.
  • President of business operations Gillian Zucker has been suspended without pay for one year.
  • President of basketball operations Lawrence Frank has been suspended without pay for six months.
  • Leonard was fined $700,000 for improper benefits.
  • Dennis “Uncle Dennis” Robertson has been banned from conducting business with NBA teams for five years, although Kawhi is his lone client.

The scale of the punishment closely mirrors, although it clearly tops it, the NBA’s response to Minnesota in 2000. More than 25 years ago, former NBA commissioner David Stern stripped the Timberwolves of five first-round picks and fined the franchise $3.5 million after determining it had entered into an illegal secret agreement with Smith. Two of Minnesota’s five picks were later returned.

The Clippers’ draft situation is particularly tough. After years of outgoing picks tied to the Paul George trade, the latest penalties leave Los Angeles of its own first-round selections under the current setup. Sheesh…

The NBA suspended Ballmer for knowingly seeking to help Leonard obtain off-court income opportunities and approving a business arrangement connected to the Aspiration endorsement. Zucker was cited for being directly culpable in the endorsement arrangements and for providing false and misleading statements to investigators, while Frank was disciplined for his involvement and for approving impermissible expenses involving Leonard and his family.

Funnily enough, Leonard’s punishment differed significantly from Smith’s 25 seasons earlier, as Kawhi came out pretty much unscathed. Smith’s contract was voided in 2000, while the NBA decided to leave Leonard’s contract intact and instead ordered him to pay $700,000 over improper benefits. Lots of money to us, pocket money for the Klaw.

Los Angeles “vehemently” rejected the NBA’s findings and said it intends to challenge the ruling through every available avenue. Meanwhile, Kawhi is still on his way to Canada to play basketball north of the border next season.

items.title: Several current, former Knicks ball out in FIBA World Cup Qualifiers
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
I know it’s not everyone’s cup of tea, but I do really love international basketball. Really, I love all forms of national-team events. It’s the reason I watch the World Cup religiously and ignore soccer’s existence for much of the following four years. It’s why I tune in to a lot of sports I usually wouldn’t during the Olympics, both summer and winter. Basketball is no exception, except it’s a sport I do actually watch quite a lot.

It’s a good thing this isn’t a big international basketball summer, as the Knicks are enjoying their offseason following their historic playoff run and third NBA championship. The next two summers, though, are full of it. The FIBA World Cup will take place in Qatar next summer and will determine who plays at the 2028 LA Olympics.

You do have to qualify for that, however, which is what’s gone on this summer. Dozens of countries around the globe are taking to the court in hopes of qualifying for the FIBA World Cup, a place that these nations almost have to be at to even have a chance of calling themselves Olympians.

As such, many NBA players are getting reps in this offseason overseas, particularly the Euros. Just look at Nikola Jokic and Victor Wembanyama squaring off in a heated game during a qualifer to a qualifier in the middle of the offseason:

Two current Knicks and three former Knicks* competed in the most recent window of games across the world, so let’s check in on them and how they balled out for their country:

Pacome Dadiet (Ivory Coast)

Dadiet is a native of France; that much is true, but he was born to Ivorian immigrants along the southern coast, just outside of Nice, so he elected to represent Côte d’Ivoire (Ivory Coast). This was actually his senior national team debut after playing for France as a teenager.

Ivory Coast entered the second round of qualification in a very good spot with a 5-1 record that carries over into Group F. With the window’s games being played in Dakar, Senegal, the Ivorians first squared off with Mali last Thursday, winning a narrow 83-77 result.

Dadiet, playing alongside his older brother, Maxence, for the first time, had nine points and nine rebounds, going 4-for-12 from the field and 1-for-8 from three. What the Knicks will like here are the five offensive rebounds, something the team might need some help with after the departure of Mitchell Robinson.

On Saturday, they faced off with Egypt and won another close contest, 72-66. Dadiet scored 13 points with six rebounds in 25 minutes, going 5-for-15 from the field and 3-for-7 from deep, while the team lost his minutes by 12 points.

Ivory Coast re-took the court the next day on Sunday for a game against Angola and got blown out, losing 91-70 to conclude the August window. Dadiet had 10 points, seven assists, and five rebounds across 31 minutes, going 2-for-9 from the field and missing all four of his threes. The jumper still isn’t there right now.

As with every other FIBA Qualifier, the remaining three dates will all be in the February 2027 window, meaning any NBA talent will have no control over what their country does from here. Ivory Coast sits at 7-2 and would likely only need to win one of their final three games to get to Qatar.

Jose Alvarado (Puerto Rico)

The only Olympian on the current Knicks’ roster, Alvarado played for his father’s country in Paris back in 2024 and continues to represent them on the international stage. Unfortunately for Alvarado, the prospects of getting back to Paris are increasingly slim.

Puerto Rico advanced by the slimmest of margins in Group B with a paltry 2-4 record, which unfortunately carried over into Group F play in the second round. In the two games in the August window, where Alvarado was able to participate, they could not manage a win.

The first game last Thursday against Argentina got away from them in the second half, as they lost 89-75 in Mar de Plata. Alvarado had 19 points, six rebounds, and four assists, but also committed five turnovers in 36 minutes of work, going 7-for-15 from the field and 3-for-8 from deep. As the clear focal point of the offense, he was consistently targeted.

On Monday, P.R. stayed in South America, visiting Uruguay in Montevideo and losing 80-75, falling behind early and never recovering. Once again playing considerable minutes, Alvarado was held to just three points on 1-for-9 shooting, but dished out nine assists with just two turnovers in 33 minutes of action, posting a positive plus-minus.

With four matchdays remaining in November and February, Puerto Rico is going to have to likely win at least three to have a shot at the FIBA World Cup, sitting at 2-6 with the Bahamas currently sitting in fourth at 4-4 as the last team in.

Does Dillon Jones count as a current Knick or is he an OAKAAK? The two-time NBA champion is currently a free agent, but is a strong contender to take one of the team’s open two-way spots after participating in Summer League. Nonetheless, he’s in the gray area… for now.

The state of USA Basketball is as follows. We care a lot about the Olympics; we care a bit about FIBA; we don’t give a damn about anything else. Unlike other countries, which have some of their best and brightest playing these qualifiers, Team USA is currently a smorgasbord of ex-college stars and guys with brief stints in the league. Here’s who Jones was teammates with this week. All of these would qualify as “good pulls” if you want to prove your ball knowledge:

  • Mike James – former Brooklyn Net teammate of KD and Kyrie
  • Jaron Blossomgame – 27 career games with the 2019 Cavs, All-ACC guard at Clemson
  • Cole Swider – former Laker who split time at Syracuse and Villanova in college
  • DeJon Jarreau – All-AAC guard for Houston who’s played 26 career NBA games for Memphis and Indiana
  • Kevon Harris – played 36 games for Orlando, Stephen F. Austin grad
  • Pedro Bradshaw – played college at Bellarmine and Eastern Kentucky
  • Darius Brown II – UDFA out of Utah State who played three minutes for Cleveland on February 24th
  • Tyler Smith – 33rd pick by the Bucks in 2024, 35 career games
  • Garrison Brooks – started for UNC and Mississippi State across a five-year collegiate career. Was a Knick for three days in September 2022
  • Orlando Robinson – 115 games for four teams

I mean, look at this group.

They started the August window last Thursday in Santiago against Chile, riding a Swider 19-point game to a blowout victory. Jones didn’t play much, only four minutes where he had a rebound and an assist.

Four days later, on Monday, they came home to face Colombia in Washington, D.C., where they won 102-80. Jones again played only four minutes, scoring two points with a rebound and an assist.

While already qualified for the Olympics by being the host country, the U.S. will want revenge after a terrible 2023 World Cup showing, so these are still important to them. With four matchdays remaining, the Americans are firmly on top with a 7-1 record, as close to clinched as possible. They won’t need any NBA talent for this.

Mamadi Diakite (Guinea) – Guinea went 4-2 in Round 1 and took two of their three games in the August window, with the former Knick being a big part of them being on track to compete in Qatar next summer.

He had 14-11-6 in a bad shooting game in the loss against South Sudan, but rebounded to put up 11-4-4 with five stocks in the win over Cabo Verde, while posting 12-5-5 with four stocks against Cameroon.

Diakite played seven total games as a Knick in 2023-24, including four in the postseason in garbage time, as the rotating 15th roster spot. He currently plays in Dubai.

Willy Hernangomez (Spain): There is no Knick from the late-2010s dark ages that I have more of a heart for than Hernangomez, who I believed in way too much. Spain went 5-1 in the first round and looked as formidable as ever entering Group E play, but have hit a major roadbump.

Willy, playing alongside his brother Juancho, scored seven points with two rebounds in a 95-89 loss to Portugal to open the August window, before being held off the board in just eight minutes of play in an overtime loss to a Giannis-less Greece.

items.title: Help Wanted: Join the Posting and Toasting team!
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
Hello. Do you like the Knicks? Would you like to write about the Knicks?

We here at Posting and Toasting are looking to expand our staff with a variety of different types of paid contractor positions, from people to blog the news, write game previews and recaps, weekly columns, among other possible duties. Pay rates vary based on responsibilities and experience level.

Qualifications include, but may not be limited to:

  • A genuine passion for basketball, particularly for the New York Knicks. This is easily the most important.
  • Previous writing/blogging/social media/graphic design experience, whatever is relevant to the position being applied for.
  • An ability to come up with original editorial ideas to help both drive and react to the ongoing conversation around the team. This can range from X’s and O’s, deep-dive statistical breakdowns to more column/blog-style takes on what it all actually means. Or perhaps a blend of all of the above and more.
  • An ability to accept feedback and make prompt adjustments to a story prior to publishing, and to submit work prior to deadlines.

So if you’re looking to join our crew, then fill out this form and apply! And be prepared to show examples of your prior work. We look forward to hearing from you!

items.title: The Diawara Question: Sifting through summer league noise
items.author: John Gove
items.content:
Summer League notoriously creates optical illusions. Hot shooting can spark irrational hype, while a cold stretch can trigger unnecessary panic. For Mohamed Diawara, the exhibition run landed directly into the panic bucket. Struggling to find a rhythm, the young wing looked disjointed offensively and out of sync with the game’s pace.

Of course, context changes everything. Shortly after play in Las Vegas concluded, news emerged that Diawara had played through a fracture left ring finger. After successful surgery, he has already resumed on-court workouts as he prepares for training camp.

Evaluating Diawara requires moving past one compromised Summer League performance. Behind the overdramatic noise is a long-limbed prospect with an intriguing foundation, organizational financial backing, and a defined set of benchmarks under Mike Brown.

Diawara possesses the physical build modern front offices hope to find on the wing. His long wingspan and standing reach give him the length to shrink the floor, clog passing lanes, and effectively contest perimeter shots. Positionally, he symbolizes the length-and-versatility prototype modern NBA defense demands.

During his rookie campaign, Diawara logged 69 regular-season appearances, averaging 9.2 minutes a game. While 3.6 points and 1.4 rebounds per game appear modest on paper, his underlying efficiency provides reasons for optimism. Shooting 36.9% from three, he demonstrated a reliable catch-and-shoot stroke. More importantly, he flashed against high-level competition. Against the Pelicans in December, Diawara recorded a career-high 18 points in 18 minutes, while going 4-for-4 from beyond the three-point line. Later in the season, he held his own against Jaylen Brown in Boston, demonstrating the lateral quickness necessary to stay in front of elite scorers.

Signing Diawara to a four-year, $10 million contract in June, New York’s front office signaled its belief in his potential. The team-friendly deal cements his status as a long-term developmental investment instead of a player merely fighting for a roster spot. If his ball-handling and straight-line driving improve over time, his ceiling compares to the likes of Jerami Grant or a Pascal Siakam (light). If he simply masters the role of a spot-up shooting threat, he becomes a rotational wing similar to Naji Marshall or Kyle Anderson.

When evaluating Diawara’s path for the upcoming season, expectation management is crucial. New York enters the season as defending champs, showcasing a deep, established veteran rotation. Charity minutes will not exist, leaving limited non-garbage-time minutes. Realistically, Diawara projects as developmental depth set to absorb low-leverage regular-season minutes. His primary function will be to serve as a low-cost insurance policy when veterans need a rest or sustain a minor injury. As he showed last season, he can effectively step into spot starts or ten-minute stints without derailing the offense. No one should expect Diawara to walk out of training camp as a consistent 15-to-20 minute staple. Instead, his job is to stay ready, refine his practice habits, and provide flexible floor spacing whenever match-ups demand extra size.

For Diawara to force his way into Mike Brown’s primary rotation, three distinct areas of his game must take steps forward. First, earning Brown’s trust requires total scheme discipline and faster defensive processing. He has the physical length to switch across multiple positions, but physical tools mean little if the rotational decisions are late. Diawara must demonstrate rapid awareness and avoid blown coverages by staying disciplined against perimeter pump fakes.

Second, he needs to prove he can provide high-volume floor spacing. Shooting 36.9% from deep last season established a solid foundation. However, it occurred on limited volume. To share the floor with ball-dominant creators, Diawars needs to prove his three-point efficiency holds up under higher volume and heavier defense. If defenses must respect his jumper, it stretches the floor and unlocks driving lanes.

Finally, a 1.4 rebounding average over 9.2 minutes per game is insufficient for someone with Diawara’s standing reach. In Brown’s system, defensive possessions are not complete until a rebound is secured. Diawara must play with greater urgency on the glass, utilizing his frame to box out and consistently secure contested boards.

Mohamed Diawara’s frustrating July was an injury-impacted blip. It was not a developmental setback. With finger surgery in the rearview and four years of contract security, his raw skill and attributes remain intriguing. His journey from an end-of-the-bench project to a steady rotation player depends entirely on how quickly his defensive processing catches up to his physical gifts. Whether his quickest path to consistent minutes lies as a mobile, small-ball power forward or strictly as a perimeter wing, it will be one of the most compelling developmental storylines.

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘We don’t talk about the trophy’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
We’re already into September, and that can only mean one thing: we’re back in business.

Starting today, your freshest and first Bulletin of the 2027-28 NBA season.

(Here’s a small bunch of quotes, because the calendar page might have flipped but it’s not that we’re already close to anything of importance.)

On putting last season’s championship behind entering their title defense:

“We don’t want to speak of the trophy, we don’t talk about the trophy, we don’t want to see the trophy. We want to come in with the same mindset, if not, even a tougher mindset than we had last year… It’s important for us to come into this season to be like, ‘That’s over with.’”

On modeling his early career stint in Dallas after JJ Barea:

“My mindset was, I’m filling JJ Barea’s role. He came off the bench for Dallas. He did all these great things for Dallas. That’s where I see myself. I’m gonna work to be better, but that’s where I see myself. That’s where I feel like I can help this team.

“The more you show in your role, the longer your leash gets, the more you’re able to do. People just want to say, ‘Hey, I can do this, I can do that.’ Well, do what’s asked of you first. Perfect it. Master it.”

On refusing to call himself the “King of New York”:

“I’ve never called myself the king of New York. I will never call myself the king of New York.

“Imagine I get on this call with you, right? I’m like, ‘Yo, no king of New York’s here,’ whatever, whatever. You guys are going to look like, ‘What the f**k, this dude is so self-centered.’”

On staying grounded as his profile has grown:

“I just find a way to kind of be the same because of the people around me. I have the same people I had around since high school.”

On the belief that powered the Knicks’ championship run:

“Believe. That’s one thing you got to do is believe. The way we did it, 53 years, a lot of people say we were supposed to be there but still doubted us. A lot of people thought the first round was a way out because how we started. So I guess faith, believe. We just believed in each other, we believed in what we could do and that’s what made us champions.”

On his goal of becoming a Sixth Man of the Year candidate:

“I still haven’t done what I wanted to do with my career. I got a lot of goals that I want to push for and this is probably going to be the most hard-working summer I probably put in. I want to be in the conversation of Sixth Man of the Year one day. Obviously I got to work, obviously situations where the minutes, consistency and stuff like that is always going to be a problem because I know I’m never going to pass the eye test. If you look at me, I’m not the most tallest, most athletic to the NBA world. So I just know going into a room, I got to be the most out-working person, hardest-working person and the rest will take care of itself.”

On representing the Philippines:

“When you got Filipino blood, [you] take the whole country with you, the whole pride.

“We’re doing a lot for the country and the culture.”

On Jalen Brunson being New York’s king:

“I’m happy as the mayor. Jalen Brunson is the king.”

On wanting to become Team USA’s general manager:

“One of my main goals is to be the GM of Team USA. In one of these Olympics, one of these years, I want to do that job one time.”

On the globalization of basketball and international players becoming the NBA’s best:

“Our game is global. We play basketball all around the world (…) And it’s about time. They’ve been coming into the league since the 80s. It’s just natural evolution that guys from around the world are going to assume those positions as the best players in the league.”

items.title: (Late) August P&T mailbag: Best of the worst years, all-time Knicks vs. all-time Celtics & Juju Reese
items.author: Matthew Miranda
items.content:
September beckons, bitches. Let’s mailbag.

What would your team look like if you assembled it from the stinky years of the 2000s-2010s?

In order to tackle this question, I had to settle on what exactly “2000s-2010s” meant. We talking just the awful aughts, ending with the 2009-10 season? Or the whole stinking two decades of stank? I found myself confronted by a mystery I’d never wanted to solve: who was worse, the 2000s Knicks or the 2010s Knicks?

To really get the stink marinating, I compared two nine-year abominations: the Knick teams from 2002-2010 and from 2014-2022. Combined that’s 18 seasons, 17 below .500, 16 missing the playoffs. eight losses in nine playoff games and a partridge in a pear tree. Before I give you the numbers, what does your gut tell you? Which Knicks like they were worse?

From 2002-2010 the Knicks were 279-459; adjusted for 82 games that’s 31-51. The 2014-2022 Knicks went 262-450, a 30-50 pace. The numbers wouldn’t settle this debate. Futility being in the eye of the beholder, I had to dig deep. Was there anything particularly sadder about one batch versus the other? For me, there is.

In 2013-14, New York was coming off a tremendous run the year before, plus three consecutive winning seasons and playoff appearances. Carmelo Anthony had just led the league in scoring while finishing third for MVP. J.R. Smith was top-20 in points, Jason Kidd top-20 in steals and Tyson Chandler top-10 in offensive rebounds, an All-Star and First Team All-Defense.

The writing was on the wall once Kidd retired and James Dolan strong-armed Glenn Grunwald outta town and Andrea Bargnani in, but there was reason to feel good heading into 2014. There was excitement in 2016 for the arrival of Kristaps Porziņģis. In 2019 there was hope — if not conviction — that Kevin Durant, Kyrie Irving and Zion Williamson were on their way to save the day.

The 2001-02 Knicks were post-Patrick Ewing and, not coincidentally, not good, failing to win a playoff series in 2001 for the first time since 1991. Jeff Van Gundy left, Marcus Camby and a lottery pick were soon to follow in exchange for the low point of Antonio McDyess’ career, Latrell Sprewell was almost out the door and Isiah Thomas about to walk through it. .

At least the 2010s Knicks had the precedent of the 2000s teams to slightly soften the blow. Watching their initial sinking into stinking, from winning 17 playoff series in 12 years (1989-2000) to winning a single playoff game the next dozen, didn’t merely cause despair. It was a disorienting fall from grace. The 2010s were a bad headache. The 2000s were that plus vertigo.

Without further ado, my ‘02-’10 Knick faves:

One Saturday late in my sophomore year of college, some friends and I got in on some pickup games on campus. This was the long-gone dark ages, when I was active and thin and a pretty good baller, and that day I was . The fadeaway couldn’t miss. People were calling me Jordan. It was a very small, insignificant time and place in history, and if you weren’t literally there experiencing it in real time, it makes neither sense nor difference.

So it goes with those of us who swore allegiance to the Frank Williams cult twentysomething years ago — if you weren’t there, it makes zero sense. To be fair, it didn’t make a lotta sense even if you were; Williams, a point guard, shot just 35% from the field and 30% from deep and started only three games over two years in New York. And yet if the Knicks announce tomorrow they’ve signed Williams outta retirement, I’d tell Jalen Brunson thank you for your service, now get thee to the bench. The prophecy must be fulfilled.

Crawford and Lee were that restaurant that used to be open near you that was delightfully, surprisingly good. It had no business being that good, and it closed years ago. But you appreciated it when it was there, and the memories still warm you today. Looking at you, Amy’s Place in Buffalo. R.I.P.

Kurt Thomas I loved because he was a true warrior for righteousness, willing to tangle with anybody and everybody who was in the wrong, no matter who it was. Whether that be a future Hall of Famer.

Or the biggest fish in his own pond, like in 2004 when Thomas told Knick teammate Stephon Marbury, “Everyone in this organization is afraid of you, but I’m not. I’ll beat your ass.”

Thomas joins Ewing — I think — as the only Knicks who’ve impacted winning for the club over a 14-year stretch. A key reserve for the 1999 Knicks, many of us still fondly remember the final game Thomas ever played down the stretch in 2013: the Knicks had lost a season-high four straight games and five of six as they played in Utah without Carmelo. Gutting through 27 minutes, Thomas helped the Knicks snap the losing skid and kickstart a 13-game winning streak, the finishing touch on their best season in 13 years.

I hold a special place in my heart for Dr. Michael Doleac because of December 30, 2002. I was driving from Rochester to New York City and a friend tagged along looking to visit a friend in Pennsylvania. My friend considered himself hilarious for not telling me the drinks he was downing the whole drive down were spiked; by the time I figured out he was drunk, he figured out we were lost. We were “near” enough that his friend came and got him, leaving without leaving me directions to get back toward the city. It was dark out in the middle of nowhere, Pennsylvania, pre-Google maps (the less said about Mapquest, the better).

I spent the drive low on gas, cursing my friend for my being lost in what looked like every horror movie ever and living and dying with the back and forth in WFAN’s broadcast of what ended up a one-point Knick win over the NBA champion Spurs. In arguably his finest hour as a ‘bocker, Doleac scored 16 points (two off his Knick-high) and grabbed eight boards (tying his Knick best) against Tim Duncan and David Robinson. I wanna end this with “This doctor makes house calls,” but the game was in New York. Then again, “This doctor takes patient visits” just doesn’t work at all. Gimme your best Doleac tag line.

[List your] ranking of trades/signings/moves that built the 2026 champion Knicks.

16) Drafting Pacôme Dadiet15) Signing Jeremy Sochan13) Signing Mo Diawara

12) Signing Ariel Hukporti

11) Drafting Miles McBride

10) Signing Landry Shamet

9) Drafting Mitchell Robinson

8) Trading for Mikal Bridges

7) Trading for Josh Hart

6) Signing Jalen Brunson’s first contract

5) Trading for Karl-Anthony Towns

4) Trading for OG Anunoby

3) Firing Tom Thibodeau & hiring Mike Brown

2) Signing Jalen Brunson’s second contract

1) Hiring Leon Rose

Clyde and Jalen in the backcourt with Willis, Patrick and Bernard up front. From my admittedly biased perspective, this starting five could match up with any all-time mythical squad the Celtics could put together.

DeanJose’s five vs. Bill Russell, Larry Bird, Kevin McHale, John Havlicek and Paul Pierce — who ya got??

The Wizards traded Angel Reese’s brother Julian “Juju” Reese to the Nuggets, who then released him. While he only played 13 games (10 starts) and 30.9 minutes per game, he put up respectable numbers on a tanking team (11.8 points/10.5 rebounds, including the most offensive rebounds per game since Hakeem Olajuwon at 4.2). He’s a little undersized at 6’9, 230 lbs., but seems like a decent candidate for the third-string center job. Thoughts?

First, if this is Angel Reese stanning for her , I fully understand. And email me. Please. God, please email me, Angel Reese.

Assuming this is really Stan KGRY, my only thoughts are that there are definitely dudes who’ve beaten that Olajuwon number from 1987 — Dennis Rodman did a half-dozen times by himself — and that whatever downgrade there is between Mitch and Drummond, the Knicks are probably looking to make that up with an upgrade over Hukporti. You can’t count on KAT playing heavy minutes for 82 games followed by a two-month title defense, nor do I think they want to count on Drummond being the best next man up that whole time. There is 100% room for Juju Reese to make a home and career in the NBA. I don’t see it this year in New York, though.

That’s all she wrote for the mailbag, and it’s gonna be all she wrote for a while. I’m now writing about the Knicks at OnSI, and no longer at P&T. I’ve left before and returned; this feels less like “Goodbye” than “Later.” I’ll still pop into the comments sometimes, and have a few other pots starting to boil. Email if you want. I’m on Bluesky. I love you all. Not all. But you, reading this now, I love. Yes, you.

items.title: The mysterious erasure of RJ Barrett
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
Really, how often do you remember Rowan Junior?

Mayor Zohran Mamdani did. Speaking at the Knicks’ championship ceremony at City Hall on June 18, he made sure RJ Barrett’s name was included among those who helped build the title team:

“This championship belongs to them too, because championships aren’t just built in one season. It belongs to Immanuel Quickley, RJ Barrett, Donte DiVincenzo, Julius Randle, and also to a coach who also laid the groundwork, Tom Thibodeau.”

Still, Barrett has become strangely easy to overlook when we talk about the era that began with Thibodeau, Julius Randle, and the 2020–21 “We Here” Knicks. On this date, September 1, 2022, RJ signed an extension that appeared to establish him as part of the long-term core; 16 months later, he became the central piece of the trade that brought OG Anunoby to New York.

Rowan Alexander “RJ” Barrett Jr. arrived with bona fide basketball bloodlines. His father, Rowan Barrett Sr., starred at St. John’s, played professionally overseas, captained Canada at the 2000 Olympics, and later became general manager of Canada Basketball. His mother, Kesha, was a nationally ranked sprinter and long jumper at St. John’s. Steve Nash, one of the greatest Canadian basketball players ever, is RJ’s godfather. With all that preceding him, clearly young RJ was destined to be a professional bowler.

Born in Toronto in 2000, Barrett starred at St. Marcellinus before transferring to Montverde Academy in Florida. By the end of his high school career, he was the consensus No. 1 recruit in the class of 2018, with Naismith Prep Player of the Year and Gatorade National Player of the Year honors in his trophy case.

Barrett entered Duke as the projected top pick in the 2019 draft, but his roommate Zion Williamson quickly became the main attraction in Durham. The two became close friends, referred to each other as brothers, and made history as the first freshman teammates to each average more than 20 points. Williamson’s gravitational pull (literal and figurative) pushed Barrett into the background somewhat, even as RJ set ACC freshman scoring records and earned consensus first-team All-American honors.

Meanwhile, the 2018–19 Knicks were deliberately dreadful, finishing 17–65 during the first season of the new lottery odds. Their 14% chance at Williamson turned into the third pick, with New Orleans selecting Zion and Memphis taking Ja Morant. Barrett was still considered a top-three talent and a clean fit for New York, so the Knicks pounced without hesitation. Still…he wasn’t Zion. (I still think about the woman who got the Zion Knicks tattoo ahead of draft night and wonder if she still has it…)

On draft night at Barclays Center, RJ became emotional when Adam Silver called his name, later explaining that his late maternal grandfather, a die-hard Knicks fan with Brooklyn and Jamaica roots, used to tell him he would someday play for the club. After his press conference, Barrett turned toward the cameras and declared, “Yo! I’m a Knick!” His excitement was so sweetly genuine: he wanted New York, and New York wanted him right back (but…he still wasn’t Zion…).

Barrett’s rookie season was uneven, with 14.3 points per game on inefficient shooting. Thibodeau’s arrival changed the direction of the franchise and helped Barrett find firmer footing. He averaged 17.6 points in 2020–21, improved his shooting, defended harder, and helped Randle carry New York into the playoffs for the first time since 2013.

RJ reached 20 points per game the following season and continued to start nearly every night. When the Knicks extended him in September 2022, Barrett was only 22 and still looked like a key piece in whatever New York was becoming.

The fit never completely worked, though. Barrett and Randle both did their best work inside the arc, which cramped the paint, and Barrett never became a reliable enough three-point shooter or natural enough playmaker to solve the problem (particularly after Captain Brunson arrived). He could still bully his way downhill and occasionally produce a great Garden moment. His banked-in buzzer-beater that completed a comeback against Boston in January 2022 is a recent classic. Consistency, however, remained elusive.

Then, on December 30, 2023, the Knicks sent Barrett, Immanuel Quickley, and a second-round pick to Toronto for Anunoby, Precious Achiuwa, and Malachi (Evil Donte) Flynn. Anunoby’s defense and seamless fit transformed the team almost immediately, and it quickly became a pretty lopsided trade.

For Barrett, the deal meant going home. He became a steady 20-point scorer in Toronto, showed growth as a playmaker, and continued using his strength to batter his way toward the rim. Life hit him with tragedy when his younger brother Nathan died following an illness in March 2024. Barrett stepped away from basketball before eventually returning and speaking openly about his grief: “He was my best friend…I’m always missing him. I still text him.” Our hearts went out to him and still do.

The championship story understandably centers on Brunson, Anunoby, Karl-Anthony Towns, Mikal Bridges, and Josh Hart. We love them all, but none were on the team when RJ arrived. MSG was still a sort of basketball wasteland. RJ brought some hope that someday soon, things would be different. He absorbed the expectations that came with being the third pick on a miserable team, helped the Knicks climb out of the lottery years, and supplied his share of memorable nights at the Garden. Mamdani remembered, and a few others still do. For a player once expected to become the face of the franchise, his name should come up more often.

items.title: Knicks Domino Effects: What if Jalen Brunson stayed in Dallas?
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
Domino effects are meant to start relatively small. The first two editions of the series, I feel like, encompassed that. We got really niche with the Mike Brown Kings saga and less niche with Julius Randle’s injury, but both of them required a lot of outside-the-box thinking to see directly what a reversal would’ve caused to the Knicks’ long-term hopes.

This one is anything but niche.

To wrap up this mini-series I’ve had fun with over the dog days of the summer, we’re going to look at possibly the biggest domino effect of them all, one that was scarily realistic and only didn’t occur because of the hubris of a certain front office that later made one of the worst trades in NBA history.

You saw the title. This is a scenario that Jalen Brunson, the birthday boy and the man who has exceeded every expectation and has spearheaded a revival of Knicks basketball so grand that all of us have spent way too much money on championship merch, never puts on the orange and blue.

Following his third season in Dallas, Brunson and his agents at CAA wanted to negotiate a contract extension with the Mavericks’ brass. The number that they decided on was more than reasonable for a player of his current production: four years and $55 million. After all, he was coming off finishing fourth in Sixth Man of the Year voting with plausible upward mobility.

Dallas said no. Fast forward a few months: as Brunson began what turned out to be a breakout campaign, he and his agent approached the Mavs again about the same framework and were again told no.

Brunson kept working and gradually improving to the point where the Mavs themselves approached him about the $55 million deal after the trade deadline, but at that point, he had outgrown that offer as he was barreling towards free agency. Four months later, he landed in New York on a four-year, $104 million pact.

But what if Dallas realized what they had in Brunson at either one of those points, particularly the in-season extension? What if they took a guy that the Knicks had long been looking at off the market? Such a deal would’ve been more than reasonable for their current cap structure as a sixth man or starter next to Luka Doncic, even if the fit was potentially difficult due to both of their defensive shortcomings. Frankly, it was nonsensical for them to be that blind. This was a good player.

December 1, 2021. Jalen Brunson and the Dallas Mavericks announce a four-year, $55 million extension that will begin the following season. Let’s see where the dominoes fall.

Nothing changes from this point forward on any side for the rest of the 2021-22 season. Brunson still balls out and gets on the national radar with his incredible performance in the postseason; the Knicks still miss the playoffs, etc. Instead of the media clowning the Knicks for giving Brunson a nine-figure deal in June, the offseason is spent lauding Nico Harrison and company for their wherewithal to lock down this impact player for cheap.

Of course, this creates a gigantic path of divergence for the Knicks, who were always infatuated with Brunson because of his family connections. I still think Rick Brunson gets hired onto Tom Thibodeau’s staff to replace the outgoing Kenny Payne (who had a truly disastrous tenure at Louisville). The hiring was definitely motivated by his son’s free agency, but he had also served as an assistant under Thibs in Chicago and Minnesota, so it still happens.

The real question, though, is what happens in that offseason. Our first major question revolves around the strategy for the 2022 NBA Draft, particularly with the No. 11 overall pick.

For those who don’t remember, the Knicks selected Ousmane Dieng, traded him to the Thunder in exchange for three first-round picks, traded up to No. 13 in exchange for two picks, selected Jalen Duren, and shipped him to Detroit alongside Kemba Walker in an effective salary dump. The team came out with solid assets and cleared up some cash.

The motivation behind punting a lottery pick? Signing Jalen Brunson. A later trade with Detroit shipped Alec Burks and Nerlens Noel to the Motor City and cleared up just enough space for the Villanova alum and Isaiah Hartenstein in free agency. It’s why I never cared about people saying “the Knicks traded Jalen Duren for nothing” because it’s false. You don’t get Brunson (most likely) without trading Duren, his cap hit, and the salary attached.

But with Brunson off the table and no clear reason to use cap space, the Knicks are dead set on picking in the lottery. You might think it’s as simple as drafting Dieng or Duren, but the Knicks almost certainly made both selections on behalf of the teams they were actively negotiating with. After all, if they wanted them, they wouldn’t trade them.

There were a few plans for this draft leading up to it. After the Knicks were once again denied a chance at lottery luck, they constantly rang the phones to try to trade up for Jaden Ivey. They may get over the line for this. After all, with no Brunson on the way, there are no schematic issues.

It would still be a very difficult trade to make, so I lean toward it not happening. After Ivey, they seemed quite enamored with Wisconsin guard Johnny Davis, but the Wizards took him 10th overall. That’s two major bullets dodged, but who’s on the clock at No. 11?

The available players who had a pre-draft workout in New York were AJ Griffin, Tari Eason, MarJon Beauchamp, and Mark Williams. I would think it would be one of these guys, even if the extremely talented Jalen Williams and Duren were on the board. In typical Leon Rose fashion, he probably does the first two trades of the night, where he trades out and comes back in, ultimately scooping up two conditional firsts from Detroit and Washington while trading four seconds.

With the 13th pick, they select Duke wing AJ Griffin.

With no Brunson and an unsuccessful pursuit of both Davis and Ivey in the draft, the Knicks badly need a point guard. I’d assume they still look to offload salary, particularly with Kemba, to open cap space, but the extent of this is unclear due to the lack of a clear alternative in free agency. There’s restricted free agent Collin Sexton, of course, but the direction that needs to be taken appears to be in the trade market.

Fortunately, there are two lead guards available.

Dejounte Murray is on the block in San Antonio and could be had for a reasonable package. His defensive fortitude makes him a welcome fit for a team that has major defensive questions, and his offense has also proven capable of a leap forward. There’s also that New York native out in Utah who could be of use…

For Murray, the Knicks never seemed that motivated to make that move, even if he would’ve been a decent fit next to Brunson in real life. They were always more focused on adding Donovan Mitchell and figuring it out later. In this timeline, Murray still goes to Atlanta, but it’s a full-court press on bringing Spida home.

With no Brunson, there’s nothing holding them back from adding a small guard into the fray. The fit concerns aren’t there. When Danny Ainge and the Jazz ask for a ridiculous package, it’s eventually negotiated down into something the team can agree on.

In mid-August 2022, Mitchell comes home for a package centered around RJ Barrett and Quentin Grimes, depleting the team’s draft capital to keep further players out of the deal. As much as fans want to play the kids, the Knicks see an opportunity to compete and take it.

Thus, here’s the rotation we have heading into the 2022-23 season:

Donovan Mitchell – Derrick RoseEvan Fournier – Immanuel Quickley

Alec Burks – Cam Reddish/AJ Griffin

Julius Randle – Obi Toppin

Mitchell Robinson – Isaiah Hartenstein

Yes, in this reality, we assume that the Knicks still find a way to get off Noel’s contract but keep Burks as wing depth after trading Barrett and Grimes. Hartenstein was always a target for the front office and still comes to New York.

This lineup, as you might imagine, would’ve been rather erratic. You have some brilliant shotmakers in there, but not enough defenders. Tom Thibodeau’s seat gets hot again; he’s forced to bench some players permanently, and the mini-revival still happens… to an extent.

Quickley gets a chance to start with Spida, Deuce McBride’s emergence happens a year sooner, Randle enjoys his bounce-back season. The foundation of the start of the Brunson era would’ve likely been similar, but the real repercussions come later.

At the deadline, the team needs wing depth, having iced Reddish out of the rotation. With Brunson no longer on the team, I can’t imagine the interest in Josh Hart is any more pronounced. It’s still possible that the trade happens. I’m instead going to involve the Knicks in the multi-team trade with the Warriors and Pistons that got Gary Payton II back to the Bay. The Knicks send a bucket of seconds and Cam Reddish to Detroit for Saddiq Bey.

With Mitchell, the Knicks win 48 games and slide into the fourth seed in the Eastern Conference, where they host a Cavs team that never got the New York native and instead had to continue building around Darius Garland, Sexton, and Evan Mobley. The Knicks still win in five.

In the second round, the Bucks still get slayed by the wrath of Jimmy Butler and the Heat, and although many fans are optimistic about the prospects of facing the No. 8 seed, Butler waxes the Knicks in a six-game defeat.

Heading into the following season, the Knicks are content with what they got, planning to use it as a building year. Burks never being traded means there’s not enough space to sign Donte DiVincenzo, who was also likely going to be someone Brunson pitched signing. There’s no big move to be made here, so we keep going into a shaky start to the 2023-24 season, which leaves them at an inflection point around the New Year.

As you might recall, OG Anunoby was acquired in real life on December 30, 2023, for RJ Barrett, Immanuel Quickley, and a second-round pick. In this reality, Barrett is already gone, but Quickley is becoming a foundational piece after being started out of necessity midway through the prior season. The financials still work if the Knicks add Burks to the trade, but with Barrett not included, the rest of the team’s excess draft capital goes with it.

The Big 3 of Spida-Anunoby-Randle destroy the competition in January 2024 until injuries take out both Randle and Anunoby. Mitchell does his best to imitate 2024 Brunson and gets First-Team All-NBA for his troubles, but it’s certainly an uphill climb. Without DiVincenzo to help with off-ball scoring, the Knicks only win 46 games, dropping them to the play-in tournament. Remember, the No. 2 and No. 7 seeds were just three games apart that year.

The Knicks get revenge on the Heat in the 7-8 game, but have to fare with a road series against Giannis Antetokounmpo and the Bucks in the first round, one that just doesn’t go well. With no Randle to physically match up, Toppin (who I believe doesn’t get traded with the team’s worst depth the prior season) and Precious Achiuwa are overwhelmed in a six-game defeat. The front office blames injuries and doesn’t make any drastic moves… yet.

The Mikal Bridges trade never happens. They had to use a boatload of draft assets to get Anunoby and Mitchell, so the Nets aren’t interested. Anunoby extends, Spida gets his three-year, $150 million extension, and the Knicks seem prepared to run it back in 2024-25.

Now, you might wonder: what about KAT?

The Knicks badly wanted him, but they lacked a guy who Minnesota really valued in DiVincenzo to get it done. Further, the fact that Mitchell took a max extension puts the team eerily close to the second apron, something they avoided with Brunson’s pay cut. There’s a very realistic world that this trade doesn’t happen, but Leon Rose always gets his guy, so they trade Mitchell Robinson and the last bits of draft capital to get it done.

It’s not worth prognosticating who fills the Hart and Bridges gaps in the lineup, but the Knicks are built around Mitchell, Anunoby, and Towns. That Big 3 would get two seasons to work everything out, going into the second apron in 2025-26 before James Dolan would order a restructuring. They had to win. They had no choice.

In the first year, they get bounced in the second round by the Celtics after a 52-win season. The poise of the Brunson-led Knicks was a big part of why they came back from all those deficits, plus the team would be utterly devoid of defensive length without Robinson or Bridges. This also means that the Knicks and Pacers never rekindle their rivalry in either season, which is fun to think about.

In 2025-26, the year we all rejoiced in real life, they had a real chance. They fortified the depth; they hired Mike Brown to replace Thibs; they waltzed into an extremely weak East and grabbed the bull by the horns.

50 wins in the regular season, enough for the No. 3 seed. They survived a seven-game war with Atlanta, took out Philadelphia in six games, and went face-to-face with the Pistons in the ECF. Remember, no Mitchell likely dooms the Cavs to mediocrity and no ECF berth.

It’s hard to say for sure if the Pistons give the Knicks the same fits they did in real life, but let’s look at the facts. The Knicks were still a major question mark defensively and had no answer for Cade Cunningham. Additionally, they lacked the presence of Robinson (even in a backup role) to fluster Duren. In a tense, seven-game series, the Pistons prevailed. It’s over.

Mitchell would not be extended again by the Knicks, as his playoff shortcomings would not be worth the $270 million extension he got in real life. I’d think the front office would side with the Big Bodega in this, and the team would be built around the fleeting prime of Towns from here.

Safe to say, no banners. Sad stuff. But how’s Jalen doing in Dallas?

Brunson’s New Life In Dallas

Dallas did basically nothing that offseason to replace Brunson, leaving them inherently weaker entering the 2022-23 season. They still acquire Christian Wood after retaining Brunson, but they feel pretty stagnant.

The big change in the 2022-23 season is that the Mavericks never traded for Kyrie Irving, as the fit with him, Brunson, and Luka would’ve been quite bizarre. They also wouldn’t feel the need to, as when Doncic goes down with injury right before the deadline, we see glimpses of Knicks Brunson in the emerging Villanova alum.

Dallas was quite bad this season, flaming out in the play-in tournament, but an interesting trickle-down effect from this is that they wouldn’t be able to properly tank to keep their draft pick, so a parting gift from Brunson would give the Knicks a lottery pick in 2023, which they’d use on a guy like Jordan Hawkins. Not a needle mover, so I didn’t feel the need to mention until now.

The reverb would be no Dereck Lively II in Dallas, but the supporting cast from guys like PJ Washington and eventually Daniel Gafford would provide enough for the Mavericks to still go deep in the postseason in 2024, maybe making the NBA Finals but still not coming that close to a title.

At the same time that all appears to be well in Dallas, Nico Harrison is stirring. He doesn’t like the frequent unavailability of Doncic, who still suffers a major hamstring injury on Christmas 2024. In his absence, unlike in real life where Kyrie suffered a multi-week injury as well, the Mavericks experience the joy of 2024 Jalen Brunson, who carries Dallas through January to the point where Harrison has an epiphany.

“What if I fortify my defense and Jalen can give me Luka-esque production?”

Brunson’s explosion dooms Doncic’s tenure, as the controversial trade with the Lakers still occurs. Anthony Davis would now be paired with a head of the snake in Brunson, a match seemingly made in heaven.

Except Davis is still injury-prone. Dallas never has the death spiral they had with Davis and Irving’s season-ending injuries because Brunson would be there trying to play hero ball. He does just enough to win them 45 games to take the No. 9 seed. After defeating Sacramento in the 9-10 game, a heroic 40-ball sees them stun the Grizzlies to steal a playoff spot, only to get eviscerated by the powerhouse Thunder.

This turns out to be an utter disaster, as Cooper Flagg will no longer become a Maverick. It was possible to have a core of Brunson, Davis, and Flagg, but now? Brunson hits his 30th birthday with Davis shipped to Washington and a band of merrymen around him.

That’s right. The real twist of all of this? Nobody wins.

The Knicks lose because they don’t have Brunson. They never sniff the NBA Finals.

The Mavericks lose because the domino effect takes two lottery picks away, and JB’s hyper-competitiveness doesn’t allow them to get younger.

Jalen Brunson loses. Instead of being the King of New York, he’s got a microscope on him in lowly Dallas as the guy Nico traded Luka to feature.

It’s a lose-lose situation. What a nightmare. I need my nightlight; someone turn on some highlights.

That’s better. Happy Birthday, Cap. We’re so glad this never happened.

items.title: Happy 30th Birthday, Cap!
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
Another Knick turns 30 this week! Days after Mikal Bridges reached the milestone, Captain Jalen Brunson celebrates his birthday today.

Born August 31, 1996, in New Brunswick, New Jersey, the Knicks captain hits the 30-year mark about 11 weeks after delivering New York its first NBA championship since 1973 and earning Finals MVP. Brunson capped the series with 45 points in the championship-clinching Game Five against the Spurs, a Knicks Finals record. Not a bad year so far, all things considered.

Brunson spent much of his childhood in southern New Jersey, including Cherry Hill, but his father’s basketball career kept the family moving. Rick Brunson played nine NBA seasons before transitioning to coaching, and the family eventually settled in the Chicago area, where Jalen attended Stevenson High School in Lincolnshire, Illinois. His mother, Sandra, played volleyball at Temple, where she and Rick were both student-athletes.

At Stevenson, Jalen won a state championship and Illinois Mr. Basketball honors. At Villanova, he won national championships in 2016 and 2018, then became the consensus National Player of the Year as a junior. Dallas selected him with the 33rd pick in the 2018 draft, making him the last of four Villanova teammates called—a fact most definitely not lost on the uber-competitive Jalen. Over his first four seasons, he developed from a reserve into a central figure on the Mavs team that reached the 2022 Western Conference Finals.

That summer, Jalen inked a four-year, $104 million contract with the Knickerbockers. The deal drew skepticism at the time, but Brunson quickly became the lead guard New York had spent decades seeking. He has since earned multiple All-Star and All-NBA selections, won the 2025 NBA Cup and its MVP award, and led the Knicks to the 2026 championship. On August 6, 2024, he became the 36th captain in franchise history.

Before Jalen arrived, the Knicks had made the playoffs once in the previous nine seasons. Four years later, they were champions. Rick had played for the 1998–99 Knicks, the franchise’s previous Finals team, and Jalen completed the circle by leading the orange-and-blue past the Spurs, the same team that defeated Rick’s Knicks.

The connections that brought Brunson to New York ran deep. Knicks president Leon Rose began his career as Rick’s agent and later represented Jalen. Tom Thibodeau had known Brunson since childhood through Rick’s NBA and coaching career, then hired Rick as an assistant in June 2022.

And the personal connections continue: the front office not only traded for Jalen’s BFF and Villanova teammate, Josh Hart, but also surrounded him with former teammates Bridges, Donte DiVincenzo, and Ryan Arcidiacono. Sometimes it seemed like Leon’s long game was less about Jalen and more about luring Jay Wright to the NBA.

Brunson practices his trade with strength, footwork, and deception. The 6-foot-2 left-hander changes pace, backs down larger defenders, pivots through traffic, and uses his body to create space. He absorbs contact, is a league leader in drawing charges, and is unafraid of smashing his way through much taller trees (especially French ones) or taking the game-winning shot as the clock expires. The steel in his veins and his big-shot helped make Captain Clutch the King of New York.

At 30, the mileage from that contact-heavy style will be worth monitoring, and coach Mike Brown may increasingly look for ways to preserve his champion. The injuries start to pile up as the seasons tick by: Jalen has suffered numerous ankle sprains, fractured his left hand during the 2024 playoffs, and played through a left wrist injury during the 2026 championship run before undergoing surgery in July. But his unparalleled craft should age better than a game dependent primarily on vertical explosiveness.

His 2024 extension includes a player option for 2028–29, allowing him to negotiate another contract before his 32nd birthday. By signing early rather than waiting for free agency, Jalen gave the Knicks the financial flexibility to build a championship-caliber roster around him. Reports estimated that decision left hay bales of money on the table, but he has trusted the organization to take care of him in time.
